title: Agentic AI & Agent Patterns
blurb: Tests the agent loop and what makes something agentic, the ReAct pattern, tools as the only way an agent acts, short- and long-term memory, planning and multi-agent trade-offs, the failure modes to guard against, and step limits and approval checkpoints.

refLinks.label: §36.2.2 Tool Use as the Only Way an Agent Acts

ideas.title: Failure modes and the step limit
A retry loop meets its guardrail

questions.prompt: What separates an agent from a single prompt call?
options: The model is a different architecture, trained only for agent tasks.
The model has access to at least one tool that it can call.
The prompt is longer and includes a system message about being an agent.
The model runs a loop and decides its own next action and when to stop.
questions.explanation: A single call is reason then act, once. An agent observes, reasons and acts repeatedly, choosing each step from the last result. One tool call in a fixed pipeline is tool-augmented generation, not an agent. Agents use ordinary LLMs.

questions.prompt: A pipeline always retrieves documents, then calls a summariser tool once, then returns. Is it an agent?
options: No. The steps are fixed in advance, so it is tool-augmented generation.
Yes. Any system that calls a tool counts as an agent by definition.
No, because an agent must use more than two different tools to count.
Yes, because retrieval gives it long-term memory, which only agents have.
questions.explanation: What makes something agentic is the model deciding its next step from the previous result, possibly many times. A fixed sequence of calls is a script. Tool count doesn't define it.

questions.prompt: What does the ReAct pattern add before each action?
options: A search over every tool to find the one with the best past score
A written thought, so the plan is in tokens the model can condition on
A human approval step, so no action at all runs without a person's sign-off
A second model that checks whether the action is allowed
questions.explanation: ReAct is chain-of-thought applied to action choice: Thought, Action, Observation, repeat. The written thought gives the model a place to plan and correct course. Approval steps are a separate safety control.

questions.prompt: How do modern tool-calling APIs relate to the original ReAct paper?
options: They replace ReAct entirely, because the model no longer reasons before it acts.
They add a hidden planner model that ReAct did not have.
They are unrelated. ReAct is for search engines, not for language models.
The text output is the reasoning and the tool_use blocks are the actions, the same pattern at the API level.
questions.explanation: The chapter says tool-calling APIs formalise the loop, but the pattern is identical to ReAct's plain-text scratchpad. The model still writes its reasoning before choosing an action.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter call tool scoping the primary safety control for an agent?
options: Scoped tools run faster, which keeps the loop inside its step limit.
Tool scoping is required by every tool-calling API before the first call.
The model reads tool names to decide its own permissions at run time.
An agent can only act through its tools, so they bound what it can do and the damage it can cause.
questions.explanation: An agent has no abilities beyond its tools. A calculator can at worst return a wrong number. A tool that deletes files or sends money can at worst do that for real.

refLinks.label: §36.2.2 Tool Use as the Only Way an Agent Acts

questions.prompt: What is Procedure 36.1's common mistake when writing a tool description?
options: Writing the description in the second person instead of the third
Saying what the function does but not when to use it
Making the description longer than one line of text
Listing required parameters in the description as well as the schema
questions.explanation: The model chooses among tools from their descriptions. Without a triggering condition ("use this whenever the user asks about weather"), it lacks a signal to choose. The weather tool's description in Listing 36.1 includes both.

questions.prompt: In Listing 36.3, the agent calls send_email and the reviewer types "yes". What happens?
options: The program crashes, because "yes" isn't one of the two valid options it offers.
The agent asks again until it gets "y" or "N".
The email is not sent, because only "y" counts as approval.
The email is sent, because "yes" starts with "y".
questions.explanation: The check is approval.strip().lower() != "y". "yes" is not equal to "y", so the function returns "Action was not approved by the human reviewer." Any answer but y declines, which is the safe default.

questions.prompt: Which tool calls does Procedure 36.3 say need a human approval checkpoint? Select all that apply.
options: Evaluating an arithmetic expression
Sending an email
Deleting data
Making a purchase
questions.explanation: The procedure targets calls with real-world side effects: email, purchases, deletion and deploying code. A calculator has no side effects, so its worst case is a wrong number.

questions.prompt: What is an agent's short-term memory?
options: A cache of tool results kept on disk between separate runs
A vector store of the agent's past runs, searched with a memory tool whenever the agent needs to recall something
The context window, holding the running transcript of thoughts, actions and observations
The model's weights, updated after each step of the loop
questions.explanation: Short-term memory is the transcript in context. It is free but bounded. Long-term memory is the vector store searched through a tool. Weights don't change during an agent run.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter say an agent gets long-term memory?
options: Through fine-tuning after each run, so the weights hold what happened
Through a search_memory tool backed by a vector store of its own past interactions, which is RAG
Through a larger context window, which keeps every past run in the prompt
Through a separate memory model that runs in parallel with the agent
questions.explanation: To the model, recalling something from three days ago and retrieving a support ticket are the same: a tool call that returns text. A bigger window still fills up and doesn't persist across runs.

questions.prompt: How does plan-and-execute compare with iterative ReAct-style planning?
options: It is the same thing as ReAct with a lower step limit.
It is always faster, because it calls the model only once for the whole task.
It adapts better to surprising observations, but is much harder to put in front of a human reviewer.
It is more predictable and easier to review, but adapts less if an early assumption is wrong.
questions.explanation: Plan-and-execute writes the whole plan up front, which suits a human checkpoint. ReAct decides one step at a time, adapting better but risking wandering. The second option describes ReAct.

questions.prompt: A team wants a supervisor agent with four worker agents for a task one agent might handle. What does the chapter advise?
options: Use a framework like CrewAI, since hand-rolled loops can't be multi-agent.
Default to one well-scoped agent, and split only with evidence that it has become the bottleneck.
Use the multi-agent design, since more agents always means better results on any task worth automating.
Use the multi-agent design, but limit each worker to one step each.
questions.explanation: Multi-agent setups multiply latency, cost and failure points. The chapter says a single well-scoped agent beats them on most tasks. Split when context or tool surface is the proven bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Why must every agent loop have a hard step limit?
options: Tool-calling APIs refuse to run more than a fixed number of tool calls per session.
Step limits make the model reason more carefully on each step it takes.
Each step makes the model's weights drift a little, so long runs damage the model.
An ambiguous tool result can make the model retry forever instead of giving up.
questions.explanation: Infinite or near-infinite loops are the first failure mode the chapter lists. The worked example shows the limit turning an endless retry into a bounded, flagged failure. Weights don't change during a run.

questions.prompt: Why does run_agent in Listing 36.2 return "step_limit_reached" as its own status?
options: Because Python can't raise an exception from inside a for loop.
So downstream code and reviewers can tell an answered task from one that ran out of steps.
Because the trajectory is lost from memory unless a status string is returned alongside it at the end.
So the agent can restart itself automatically with twice the step budget.
questions.explanation: The procedure's key idea: make running out of steps a distinct, explicit outcome, not an exception or a silent cutoff. "Answered" and "unknown" must not look the same.

questions.prompt: What does "compounding errors" mean for an agent?
options: A wrong observation early on becomes context for every later step, so the error grows.
Two agents correct each other's mistakes, so errors cancel over time.
The step limit compounds with the context limit, which stops the agent far earlier than planned.
Each tool call costs more than the one before it, so the bill compounds.
questions.explanation: An early mistake isn't contained. Every following step reasons from it. Cost grows roughly linearly with steps, about ten calls for ten steps, which is a separate failure mode.

questions.prompt: Each agent step is a full model call. If one call costs 1 unit, about how many units does a 10-step trajectory cost?
questions.explanation: The chapter says a ten-step trajectory costs roughly ten times a single prompt call. Every step pays for a full call, so cost and latency grow with steps.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, how many times did the loop call flaky_search before stopping, with max_steps = 6?
questions.explanation: The scripted policy retried on every "No definitive result" observation, so it used all six steps and returned step_limit_reached.

questions.prompt: Why does the worked example use a scripted policy instead of a real LLM?
options: So every step is real, reproducible and measured, not a made-up transcript of what a model would say
Because a real LLM would never retry an ambiguous result
Because real LLMs can't call tools in a loop at all without a framework like LangGraph to manage it
Because the calculator tool only accepts input from deterministic code
questions.explanation: A deterministic stand-in makes the loop mechanics exact and repeatable. Real LLMs can run loops by hand, and they can retry ambiguous results, which is the failure the example models.

questions.prompt: With the same loop code, the calculator task finished in 1 step and the search task hit the limit. What made the difference?
options: The tool's observation. A clean result let the policy stop, and an ambiguous one never did.
The calculator ran on a faster machine, which finished before the timeout.
The loop logic, which handles calculator calls differently from search calls.
The step limit, which was set much higher for the calculator task than for the search task.
questions.explanation: The chapter stresses the loop was identical. Only the tool's result differed. The search never produced a result clean enough to stop on, so no stopping condition was reached.

questions.prompt: A production agent sometimes hits its step limit on vague search results. Which fix fits the chapter's three sources of agent failure?
options: Raise the step limit to 100, so the agent rarely runs out of steps.
Give it a clear stopping rule, such as answering "unknown" after two ambiguous results, and keep the hard limit.
Remove the step limit, so the agent can keep trying until the search finally succeeds.
Add three more agents to search in parallel, so one of them eventually finds a result.
questions.explanation: The mental model names a missing or wrong tool, a missing stopping condition, and compounding errors. This is a missing stopping condition, so add one and keep the guardrail. Raising or removing the limit just burns more calls, and multi-agent setups multiply cost.

bookExercises.prompt: Write the agent loop (`observe → reason → act → observe → ...`) and contrast it with a single prompt call in one sentence.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `observe → reason → act → observe (result of that act) → reason → act → ... → stop`. A single prompt call is just `reason → act`, executed exactly once. An agent runs the full loop repeatedly, with the model deciding when to stop rather than stopping automatically after one turn.

bookExercises.prompt: State Procedure 36.2's "key idea" about `step_limit_reached`, and explain why treating it as a silent cutoff instead would be a problem.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `step_limit_reached` should be a distinct, explicit return value, not an exception or a silent cutoff. Treating it as a silent cutoff would make it impossible for downstream code or a human reviewer to distinguish "the agent found the answer" from "the agent ran out of steps and the true answer is unknown." The two cases look identical without an explicit status flag, risking a partial or non-answer being treated as a confirmed result.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 36.4's measured trajectory (6 identical retries, `step_limit_reached` after exactly `max_steps=6`), explain what would have happened without Procedure 36.2's guardrail in place, using this chapter's Failure Modes section.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Without Procedure 36.2's guardrail, the scripted policy shown in Listing 36.4 would call `flaky_search("population of Atlantis")` indefinitely. It retries unconditionally whenever the observation contains "No definitive result," and that observation never changes across calls, so there is no condition inside the policy itself that would ever cause it to stop. This is exactly the "infinite or near-infinite loop" failure mode from Failure Modes. A tool returning an ambiguous, unsatisfying result with no built-in escape causes indefinite retrying rather than the model (or here, the scripted policy) giving up.

bookExercises.prompt: Comparing the two Worked Example trajectories (6-step failure vs. 1-step success using the identical loop code), explain what this comparison demonstrates about where agent failures actually originate, per Mental Model's three-place debugging list.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Mental Model's three-place debugging list is: a missing or wrong tool, a missing stopping condition, or an early error that compounded uncaught. The two Worked Example trajectories used identical loop code, identical tool implementations, and differed only in the tool's returned observation. The calculator's clean numeric result satisfied the policy's stopping condition on step 1, while `flaky_search`'s unsatisfying result never did. This demonstrates that the failure originated specifically at the "missing stopping condition" layer (the ambiguous observation gave the policy no way to recognize it should stop) rather than a tool being wrong or an early error compounding: a useful isolation when debugging a real trajectory, since it points directly at reviewing what conditions the policy/model treats as "done."

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague wants to build a five-agent system (planner, researcher, coder, reviewer, deployer) for a task that's currently handled by one well-scoped agent with three tools. Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the two or three sentences you'd say before agreeing to that redesign.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Before splitting into five agents, is there concrete evidence the single agent's context or tool surface has actually become a bottleneck? Has it hit context limits, or do the three tools genuinely require distinct specialised reasoning that's getting muddled in one system prompt? This chapter's guidance is to default to one agent and only add more with demonstrated need, because multi-agent systems multiply latency, token cost, and the number of places a failure can occur. Five agents sounds more sophisticated, but a single well-scoped agent outperforms multi-agent setups on most tasks people reach for one on."

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter's Worked Example used a deterministic scripted policy instead of a real LLM. Explain what specifically about the step-limit guardrail's *behaviour* is legitimately demonstrated by this substitution, and what would NOT be legitimately demonstrated (i.e., what a real LLM-driven trajectory could show that this one cannot).
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Legitimately demonstrated: the loop mechanics themselves. How the step counter increments, how the trajectory is logged, how the `step_limit_reached` status triggers precisely at `max_steps`, and how an unconditional retry policy genuinely exhausts the guardrail rather than stopping early. This is real, measured, reproducible behaviour of the actual guardrail code. NOT legitimately demonstrated: anything about how a real LLM would actually decide whether to retry. A real model might recognize "No definitive result found. Sources disagree." as a signal to try a *different* query, rephrase, ask a clarifying question, or give up gracefully with a caveat, none of which the deterministic scripted policy is capable of, since it has no actual judgment, only a fixed rule.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about the debate/critique multi-agent pattern mentioned in Exposition. Identify one specific type of error it's well-suited to catching that a single-pass agent would likely miss, and explain why the roughly-doubled cost might still be worth it for that specific error type.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Debate/critique is well-suited to catching a plausible-but-wrong answer that "sounds right" on a single pass but doesn't survive scrutiny, e.g., a subtly incorrect calculation or a claim that omits a caveat a careful reviewer would flag, since a single-pass agent has no mechanism to second-guess its own output once generated, while a critique step specifically prompts a second agent (or role) to look for exactly this kind of flaw. The roughly-doubled cost can be worth it specifically for high-stakes outputs where a subtle, hard-to-catch error would be expensive if it shipped uncaught. The cost of a second pass is small relative to the cost of a wrong answer reaching production undetected.
